name: Koodiyattam
summary: Koodiyattam is Kerala's ancient Sanskrit theatre tradition, known for codified acting, subtle eye gestures and temple koothambalams; a living classical ritual drama.
description: Koodiyattam (sometimes spelled Kutiyattam) is the oldest surviving form of Sanskrit theatre practised in Kerala. It preserves highly codified acting techniques, slow, detailed abhinaya (expressive acting), and a ritual performance setting in temple koothambalams.

The form matters as a continuous living link to ancient Indian dramaturgy and the Natyashastra: it combines text, music, mizhavu percussion and precise facial and eye work taught traditionally in gurukula-style schools and modern institutions.

Visitors encounter long, intense performances (sometimes spread across days), ornate costumes and the distinctive mizhavu drum; performances today appear both in temple koothambalams and at cultural centres and festivals that aim to widen audiences while safeguarding tradition.
highlights: Highly codified facial, eye and hand gestures (abhinaya)
Mizhavu percussion and slow, meditative pacing
Living gurukula training alongside institutional teaching (Kalamandalam, Nepathya, Margi)

sections.heading: Background
body: Koodiyattam (kutiyattam) literally means 'acting together' and links Sanskrit play-texts to Kerala’s temple performance culture. UNESCO lists 'Kutiyattam, Sanskrit theatre' on the Representative List, recognising its significance for living heritage.

Traditionally performed by Chakyar and Nangiar communities, the art combines ritual, acting manuals (attaprakaram), vocal music and the copper-mouthed mizhavu drum. Transmission has long used gurukula apprenticeship; since the 20th century formal schools and research centres also teach the form.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Attend a koothambalam (temple theatre) show or an institutional performance to see full or abbreviated plays; rare acts (like Ravananankam or Mayaseethankam) are highlights when staged in full. Expect intensely focused facial and eye work, long narrative passages and ritual elements.

Visit training centres and festivals (examples: Nepathya koothambalam events, Kerala Kalamandalam and Margi programmes) to watch demonstrations, short recitals, or lecture‑demonstrations that explain gesture, mudra and stage conventions.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Performances follow temple calendars and festival seasons and also appear at scheduled cultural festivals and institutional programmes — check the hosting koothambalam or centre before you travel. Many major performances happen in central Kerala (Thrissur/Ernakulam) and in Thiruvananthapuram at Margi or at Kerala Kalamandalam (Cheruthuruthy).

Respect temple etiquette: remove shoes where required, keep silence during abhinaya passages, and expect photography to be restricted. Timings and the length of acts vary widely — confirm details with organisers in advance.

latest.text: Kerala Kalamandalam records a milestone: Apurva Arthur becomes the first woman student to perform mizhavu arangettam at the institution, signalling changing access in associated disciplines.
Nepathya's festival concludes with contrasting stagings of Sita's abduction (Mayaseethankam and Ravananankam), emphasising outreach to younger audiences and sustained gurukula training efforts.
Nepathya's 17th Koodiyattam Festival in Moozhikkulam stages a full-length Ravananankam (Aug 19–24) and runs into early September, highlighting rare full-act presentations.

visitorInfo.bestTime: Year-round; festival seasons and winter months often have more scheduled performances — check temple and institution calendars.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Travel to Kochi, Thrissur or Thiruvananthapuram by air or rail, then take local transport to koothambalams or institutions (Nepathya at Moozhikkulam, Kerala Kalamandalam at Cheruthuruthy, Margi in Thiruvananthapuram); confirm venue details before visiting.
etiquette: Confirm dates and start times with the hosting temple or cultural centre — acts can be long and are tied to temple calendars.
Follow temple etiquette (remove shoes where required) and watch quietly; photography is often restricted — always ask permission.
If you want context, attend a lecture-demo or shorter excerpts to learn gesture vocabularies before a full-length act.
Respect that Koodiyattam is a living ritual tradition with caste and community histories — approach with curiosity and cultural sensitivity.
